messages.content: You are an expert programmer and mathematician.

Problem: Each of the integers $1,$ $2,$ $3,$ $\dots,$ $16$ is written on a separate slip of paper and these slips are placed in a pile. Jillian will randomly draw slips from the pile without replacement and will continue drawing until two of the numbers she has drawn from the pile have a product that is a perfect square. What is the maximum number of slips that Jillian can draw without obtaining a product that is a perfect square?

Solve step by step. End with: The answer is [your answer].

message.content:
For each integer \(n\), write it as

\[
n = s \cdot m^2
\]

where \(s\) is squarefree. For two numbers \(a\) and \(b\), the product \(ab\) is a perfect square exactly when \(a\) and \(b\) have the same squarefree part \(s\).

Now list the squarefree part of each number from \(1\) to \(16\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n & \text{squarefree part} \\
\hline
1 & 1 \\
2 & 2 \\
3 & 3 \\
4 & 1 \\
5 & 5 \\
6 & 6 \\
7 & 7 \\
8 & 2 \\
9 & 1 \\
10 & 10 \\
11 & 11 \\
12 & 3 \\
13 & 13 \\
14 & 14 \\
15 & 15 \\
16 & 1
\end{array}
\]

The distinct squarefree parts are

\[
1,2,3,5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15
\]

so there are \(11\) groups. Jillian can draw at most one slip from each group without getting a product that is a perfect square.

Since there are \(11\) groups, she can draw at most \(11\) slips. This is attainable by choosing one number from each group.

The answer is 11.
